text: What does a single neuron in a neural network compute?
reference_answer: A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through a non-linear activation function. The weights and bias are learned; the activation is what stops the whole network collapsing into a single linear function.

text: Why do neural networks need non-linear activation functions?
reference_answer: Because stacking linear layers gives you another linear function, no matter how many you stack. Without a non-linearity a hundred-layer network has exactly the representational power of a single layer. The non-linearity is what lets depth buy anything.
expected_points: composing linear layers yields a linear function
depth would add no representational power

non-linearity is what makes depth useful

text: Why is ReLU the usual default activation?
reference_answer: It is cheap to compute, and its gradient is one for positive inputs, so it does not squash gradients the way sigmoid and tanh do. That makes deep networks trainable. The cost is that neurons stuck on the negative side get no gradient at all and can die.

its gradient does not saturate for positive inputs
it avoids the vanishing gradient problem of sigmoid and tanh

text: What is gradient descent doing during training?
reference_answer: It measures how the loss would change with a small change to each parameter, then nudges every parameter a little way in the direction that reduces the loss. Repeating that over many batches walks the parameters downhill towards a minimum.
expected_points: it computes the gradient of the loss for each parameter

the step size is the learning rate

text: What is a loss function?
reference_answer: A single number measuring how wrong the model's predictions are on the data it has just seen. Training is the process of minimising it, so the loss is what actually defines what the model is trying to do — the objective is the loss, not your intention.
expected_points: it quantifies how wrong the predictions are

text: What's the difference between an epoch and a batch?
reference_answer: A batch is the group of examples processed before one parameter update. An epoch is one complete pass over the whole training set, which is many batches. You update weights once per batch, not once per epoch.

text: What does dropout do?
reference_answer: During training it randomly switches off a fraction of the units in a layer on every step, so the network cannot rely on any single unit and has to spread the representation out. It is turned off at inference time, when the full network is used.

text: What is backpropagation?
reference_answer: It is the chain rule applied backwards through the network. A forward pass computes the loss, then gradients are propagated from the output back through each layer, reusing the downstream gradient at every step so the whole thing costs about as much as one forward pass.
expected_points: it applies the chain rule backwards through the layers

text: Why use cross-entropy rather than squared error for classification?
reference_answer: Cross-entropy penalises confident wrong answers very heavily, and paired with a softmax its gradient is simply the predicted probability minus the target. Squared error gives tiny gradients when the model is confidently wrong, which is exactly when you need a large correction.
expected_points: cross-entropy heavily penalises confident errors

text: What does softmax do?
reference_answer: It turns a vector of raw scores into a probability distribution — every value positive and the whole thing summing to one. It exponentiates each score and normalises, so larger scores dominate and the relative ordering is preserved.
expected_points: it converts raw scores into a probability distribution

text: What is the vanishing gradient problem?
reference_answer: Gradients are multiplied together as they propagate backwards. If each factor is smaller than one, the product shrinks exponentially with depth, so early layers receive almost no gradient and stop learning. Saturating activations like sigmoid make it much worse.

text: What is transfer learning, and why does it work?
reference_answer: You start from a model already trained on a large dataset and adapt it to your task. It works because the early layers learn general features — edges, textures, basic language structure — that transfer across tasks, so you only have to learn what is specific to yours.

text: What is data augmentation and when does it help?
reference_answer: It expands the training set by applying transformations that change the input but not the label — flips and crops for images, paraphrasing for text. It helps most when data is limited, and it teaches the model which variations it is supposed to ignore.

text: Why use a convolutional layer instead of a fully connected one on images?
reference_answer: Because it shares one small set of weights across every position, which cuts the parameter count enormously and builds in the assumption that a pattern means the same thing wherever it appears. A fully connected layer would have to learn that separately at every pixel.

text: How does Adam differ from plain stochastic gradient descent?
reference_answer: Adam keeps running averages of both the gradient and its square, and uses them to give every parameter its own effective step size. That makes it converge quickly with little tuning. Plain SGD with momentum often generalises slightly better but needs a carefully chosen schedule.

text: What problem do residual connections solve?
reference_answer: They give the gradient a path that skips the layers entirely, so it reaches early layers without being repeatedly multiplied down. That is what makes very deep networks trainable — before them, adding layers past a point made both training and test error worse.

text: What does an attention mechanism compute?
reference_answer: For each position it scores how relevant every other position is, turns those scores into weights with a softmax, and returns a weighted sum of their values. So each position builds its representation from whichever parts of the input matter to it, rather than from a fixed window.

text: Why did transformers displace recurrent networks for sequences?
reference_answer: A recurrent network processes tokens one at a time, so training cannot be parallelised across the sequence and long-range information degrades over many steps. Self-attention connects every position to every other in one step and processes the whole sequence at once.

text: When would you use layer normalisation instead of batch normalisation?

text: What problem does the gating in an LSTM solve?
reference_answer: A plain recurrent network overwrites its hidden state at every step, so information from far back is lost and gradients vanish. Gates let the network decide what to keep, what to discard and what to expose, giving the cell state a nearly additive path through time.
expected_points: a plain RNN overwrites its state each step

text: Why does weight initialisation matter?
reference_answer: The scale of the initial weights determines whether activations and gradients grow or shrink as they pass through the layers. Too small and the signal vanishes with depth, too large and it explodes. Schemes like Xavier and He pick the variance so it stays roughly constant.
expected_points: initial scale controls how signals propagate through depth

text: What changes when you increase the batch size?

text: Why does batch normalisation behave differently at inference?

text: How does data-parallel training work across several GPUs?

reference_answer: When the new dataset is small. Fine-tuning everything on a few thousand examples overfits and destroys the pretrained features. Freezing the backbone and training only a head is the safe default, and you unfreeze progressively as you get more data.

text: What is catastrophic forgetting?
reference_answer: When a network trained on a new task loses what it knew about an earlier one, because nothing in the new objective preserves the old behaviour and the weights simply move. It is the reason sequential fine-tuning degrades the original capabilities of a model.

text: What does mixed precision training buy you, and what is the risk?
reference_answer: Half precision halves memory and runs much faster on tensor cores, so you can fit bigger batches. The risk is numerical: small gradients underflow to zero in half precision, which is why loss scaling exists and why master weights are kept in full precision.

text: Why is self-attention expensive for long sequences, and what can be done?

The usual answers are to restrict attention to a local window, to attend to a sparse or learned subset, or to use a kernel-based approximation that avoids forming the full matrix.

text: What is gradient accumulation and when do you need it?
reference_answer: Running several small batches and summing their gradients before updating, so the update behaves like one large batch. You need it when the batch size you want does not fit in memory - it buys effective batch size at the cost of wall-clock time.

text: What does an embedding layer actually do?
reference_answer: It is a lookup table mapping each discrete item to a learned dense vector. Mathematically it is a one-hot vector times a weight matrix, but implemented as an index lookup because everything else in that product is zero. The vectors are learned with the rest of the network.

text: What is pooling for in a convolutional network?

text: What does label smoothing do?
reference_answer: Instead of training towards a target of exactly one for the true class, it targets something slightly less and spreads the remainder over the others. That stops the network driving logits arbitrarily high to chase a probability it can never reach, which improves calibration.
expected_points: the target probability is softened from one

text: Why does shuffling matter for stochastic gradient descent?
reference_answer: Because each step follows the gradient of one batch, and if batches are ordered by class or by time the model is pulled towards whatever that batch contains and then pulled back. Shuffling makes each batch an unbiased sample, so the noisy steps average towards the true gradient.
